_note: Reported news for the PDF. Compiled every Sunday from the climate-news monitor sources (Eye Radio, Radio Tamazuj, Sudans Post, UN/UNMISS, ReliefWeb, Radio Yei, others); last compiled 2026-11-10 and verified 10 times against the article links. 'counties' lists every county the item names; items with no county go in scope 'national' (state or countrywide). Items older than NEWS_DAYS (21) are dropped. 'compiled' and 'verified_passes' are written only after all verification passes finish; the county bulletin workflow (news_gate.py) holds the weekly email and the social posts until they show this week's compile.

items.text: Eye Radio reports that farmers and officials in parts of Eastern Equatoria describe crop losses from drought and heat: Cooperative Ochano, head of the Magwi farmers' association, said heat destroyed maize and sorghum crops and the situation could worsen if nothing is done; the article names Lafon among the affected areas and quotes farmer Efuk Barnabas as saying farms were destroyed near harvest and people were living on wild fruits; and Juma Buhkari, CEO of Kapoeta South Municipal, said drought destroyed crops and, in his account, families were selling gold to buy cereals. The article cites a FEWS NET September update saying some eastern and southeastern areas received less than 60 per cent of normal rainfall, notes that the Warrap state government declared a state of disaster and humanitarian emergency across all its counties on 7 September, and says El Nino is not the only factor.

MSF warns that funding cuts and aid withdrawals have left about 150,000 displaced people in the Bentiu (Unity State) and Malakal (Upper Nile State) camps at risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases; MSF found roughly 60 people sharing one functioning latrine in Bentiu camp, which has about 111,000 residents. The article says Rubkona County, where Bentiu is located, accounted for nearly one-third of the more than 14,000 cholera cases recorded nationwide from January to September, and that MSF vaccinated 102,251 people in Bentiu in September. It names no county for Malakal and says Bentiu camp is in a flood-prone area but gives no details of a recent flood.

WHO's weekly situation update for 26 October-1 November lists Fangak, Renk, Rubkona and Mayom as the four counties with an active cholera response and says Fangak cases are rising. It points to a 30-day knock-out plan running 26 October-24 November and an earliest end-of-outbreak declaration on 25 November, which is a target and not a declaration.

Sudans Post reports that the government is advancing a plan for a proposed 94 km dyke between Bor South and Twic East counties in Jonglei State, discussed during a 2 November visit to Bor by a Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation delegation led by Undersecretary Sultan Lam Tungwar Kueigwong, who described the design as environmentally and animal-friendly and said it would include culverts and wildlife crossings. The article gives no funding source or construction timeline for the dyke.

items.scope: Sudd wetlands and southern and southeastern South Sudan
items.text: The FEWS NET Global Weather Hazards Summary for 5-11 November 2026 says inundation continues in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan, that a large part of western Eastern Africa faces dryness after persisting below-average rainfall over the past 90 days, and that southern and southeastern South Sudan have already experienced deteriorated vegetation conditions, which have resulted in droughts in the region; it says El Nino continues to strengthen.

Children adopted a declaration at a children's climate consultation in Juba on Thursday, calling on the government and world leaders ahead of COP31 in Turkiye for climate-resilient schools, accessible early warning systems, emergency shelters and predictable funding for community-based adaptation. Save the Children South Sudan is finalising an assessment of climate-related loss and damage across several states, focused on flooding effects on children. Payai Manyok John, the ministry's climate change director, said the government was pursuing a US$25 million proposal with UNDP, alongside plans for a further US$15 million for small-scale farmers; the article stresses these are proposals, not secured or disbursed funds, and notes ministry work on nature-based solutions and recovery in flood-affected areas of Jonglei and Unity states.

The OCHA South Sudan Humanitarian Update for 16-30 October says the FEWS NET Science Team's 23 October assessment described June-September 2026 as the driest such season in the record beginning in 1981, with more than 80 per cent of the country in extreme or exceptional meteorological drought; satellite monitoring still recorded 33,018 km2 of inundation by mid-October, down from 41,111 km2 in August. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) is projected in 40 counties and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) in 32 counties from October 2026 to January 2027, and government estimates put more than 4 million people as affected by failed rains. Local authorities in Lafon County (Eastern Equatoria) reported hunger-related deaths after widespread crop failure; prolonged dry conditions in Nasir County (Upper Nile) forced families to move closer to water; and the Greater Pibor Administrative Area declared a drought emergency across eight counties (counties not named).

The OCHA South Sudan Humanitarian Update for 16-30 October says the cholera outbreak continues to decline but localized transmission persists: as of 21 October, 112,323 cumulative cases and 1,728 deaths across 55 counties (case fatality rate 1.5 per cent). Between 15 and 21 October, 40 new cases and no deaths were reported in Fangak (26), Renk (7), Rubkona (4) and Mayom (3); over 22 September-21 October the highest caseloads were in Renk (79), Fangak (59), Rubkona (39) and Mayom (31), and Mayom had the highest case fatality rate at 6.5 per cent. The earliest possible outbreak-over date cited is 18 November 2026, a conditional projection and not an official declaration.

items.scope: Jonglei, Unity and Upper Nile states
items.text: The UK has provided 2.1 million pounds (US$2.8 million) to FAO and WFP to expand anticipatory action in South Sudan; the joint FAO-WFP news release, as quoted by Radio Tamazuj, says the funding will enable anticipatory flood interventions in Jonglei, Unity and Upper Nile states, and the article lists activities including early-warning support, anticipatory cash assistance, livelihood protection, labor-intensive public works and prepositioning of supplies, running until March 2027; the article describes the wider threat as El Nino-induced drought and flood conditions.

Radio Tamazuj reports that the Lakes State government has declared a state of disaster after drought devastated crops, raising fears of severe food shortages in the coming months; caretaker governor Riny Tueny Mabor urged households to stock food rather than wait for donors, and State Information Minister William Koji Kerjok appealed to international donors and humanitarian agencies for urgent help and warned the crisis could deteriorate into famine without immediate intervention.

The FEWS NET Global Weather Hazards Summary for 29 October-4 November 2026 says inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists, while large 90-day rainfall deficits caused abnormal dryness across South Sudan and neighbouring areas and drought-driven deterioration of vegetation was observed over South Sudan. It also forecasts abnormal heat in western South Sudan for the coming week, and notes that El Nino continues to strengthen.

Lakes State says it is working with authorities in Central and Western Equatoria to allow pastoralists to temporarily move livestock there in search of water and grazing land amid worsening dry conditions; the state government, which declared a state of disaster after prolonged dry spells, attributes the dry conditions to El Nino weather patterns and appealed to the international community for urgent life-saving assistance to prevent a potential famine.

UN Deputy Special Representative, Resident Coordinator ad interim and Humanitarian Coordinator Ramanathan Balakrishnan, at a high-level ministerial ad hoc committee meeting on durable solutions for displaced communities in Bentiu, said persistent high water levels and a possible super El Nino could increase flood risks in the area, and said what may have been viewed as a longer-term contingency has to be treated as an immediate preparedness priority; the article's lead says the UN warns Bentiu could face severe flooding sooner than anticipated. Kuyok Abol Kuyok, a caretaker minister speaking for the humanitarian affairs minister, cited recurrent flooding, limited financial resources and inadequate resilient infrastructure among the challenges and called for investment in drainage, raised roads and flood protection (county inferred from Bentiu).

The South Sudan Meteorological Service forecasts, for 20 to 28 October, rainfall of 50 to 100 mm in parts of Central and Western Equatoria, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Warrap, Lakes, Unity and Jonglei states, as well as parts of the Pibor Administrative Area and Eastern Equatoria, and says the forecast covers areas including Lainya, Yei, Morobo and Kajo-Keji in Central Equatoria; it warns communities and road users in areas expecting heavier rainfall to remain alert to possible waterlogging, localised flooding and damage or disruption to roads and bridges.

UK Ambassador Rebecca Fabrizi announced an additional 2.35 million pounds to mitigate El Nino-related risks in South Sudan, without saying which communities would benefit or when the money would be disbursed; the article also cites a FEWS NET report published in October 2026 that warns El Nino-related rainfall deficits could reduce the 2026 harvest and worsen food consumption gaps, and that identifies Jonglei and southern Upper Nile as areas where the combined effects of climate shocks and conflict could have particularly severe consequences.
